## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

## 2. Reconcile this task's tracker

**Only a run that changed something reaches the tracker.** What counts is a triage action actually taken —
an issue closed, a comment posted — or something this run leaves for a human. `left` and

  for a human. The body is the live picture — it replaces yesterday's, it doesn't accumulate.

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.

- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**

Plan body is append-only once implementation starts: divergences and new steps go in comments/sections below, never as edits to what's here.

Phases are ordered by what blocks, not by subject: human setup first, then one stacked-PR review pass per deliverable group, then execution steps that need nobody present.

## Phase 0 — out-of-band human setup

- [ ] All boxes in #5 checked.

Exit: #5 closed. Only the App-Store-facing boxes block Phase 2; none block Phase 1, so Phase 1 starts immediately.

## Phase 1 — client MVP, one stacked-PR pass

All agent-executable; lands as a stack of PRs reviewed together, base-first merge. Device spikes come first because their outcome can reshape the stack (risks R2/R4).

- [ ] **Spike (throwaway branch, results as an issue comment here):** on a real iPad — SoundAnalysis built-in classifier during a screen-locked background recording session; 60-min record+classify battery/thermal reading. Exit: measured numbers posted; go/no-go on live classification recorded.
- [ ] PR: Xcode project scaffold (SwiftUI, iPadOS 17 floor, background-audio entitlement, CI build on GitHub Actions) + `dev/requirements/` executable-spec skeleton with coverage gate red-by-default, seeded from `dev/design/setlist-requirements.md`.
- [ ] PR: Library module — jokes, sets, shows; local store.
- [ ] PR: Capture module — AVAudioEngine session, AAC file write, SoundAnalysis laugh events, monotonic tap/laugh timestamping.
- [ ] PR: Stage module — stage-mode screen per mockups (current joke, pacing bar, countdown, 3×3 grid, manual card-tap segmentation).
- [ ] PR: Review module — post-show bit timeline with laugh alignment; joke-take comparison on manual boundaries.
- [ ] PR: App Store compliance — consent + recording indicator (Guideline 2.5.14), `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`, privacy labels ("stays on your iPad"), app icon, screenshots.

Exit: stack merged; `main` green with the coverage gate bijective over the authored leaves; a release build archives in CI.

## Phase 2 — App Store execution (no code review, runnable in one sitting)

- [ ] Upload build to TestFlight internal (no Beta App Review; minutes).
- [ ] Owner smoke-tests a real set recording on their iPad.
- [ ] Submit for App Review; respond to rejections as corrections on this issue.

Exit: app live on the App Store.

## Phase 3 — backend pipeline + QR share, second stacked-PR pass

- [ ] PR: Cloudflare scaffold — wrangler config, D1 schema (`shows`, `segments`, `takes`, `laugh_events`, `share_links`), R2 buckets, deploy workflow in CI.
- [ ] PR: API Worker — presigned upload URLs, show registration, status, share-link mint/revoke; device-scoped token auth.
- [ ] PR: Container image — ffmpeg probe/chunk + Gillick laughter-detection over a full show; R2 artifacts out.
- [ ] PR: Workflow `process-show` — probe → chunked Whisper (workers-ai, timestamps re-offset) → laugh-detect → laughter+embedding segmentation with LLM bit naming → persist → publish.
- [ ] PR: Share page — static assets + R2 range-request playback, segmented set with laugh timeline, revocable slugs, App Store footer link.
- [ ] PR: App Share module — background upload, processing status, share sheet with on-device QR.

Exit: stack merged; a real uploaded show processes end-to-end on production Cloudflare; a QR scanned from a second device plays the segmented show.

## Phase 4 — quality evaluation (execution, no gate)

- [ ] Labeled laugh benchmark on ≥2 real recorded sets; Gillick vs SoundAnalysis events scored against hand labels (risk R1); detector calibration decision recorded on this issue.
- [ ] Empirical Workers AI Whisper input ceiling + chunk-stitch quality check; decision D6 resolved and recorded.

Exit: both results posted here; follow-up issues filed for whatever they demand.

Phase C of the architecture (cross-show analysis, autodetect live mode, sync) is deliberately not planned here — it gets its own tracking issue once Phase B data exists.

# over the queue. ONE RUN PERFORMS ONE ITEM (§15.22), and the queue drains as a
# chain of runs: the scheduler run dispatches this workflow every hour, a run that settled
# its item dispatches the next, and the continuation job below covers a run that
# died before it could. It carries NO cron of its own — the scheduler run's hourly dispatch
# is the guaranteed delivery, so a lost `task:ready` label event is latency lost
# and never work lost.
#
# THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE SECRETS LIVE (DESIGN §14). The wiring converge stamps
# every task's declared `required_secrets`, plus each configured invocation
# endpoint's token secret, into the step env below by name — the scheduler run and the
# janitor get none, because they never execute task code. Code-work is the only task
# code that ever sees a value; the agent hop carries nothing.
#
# MORE CAPACITY IS MORE EXECUTORS. Nothing enumerates them and each claim is
# independently leased, so a second job, a matrix width, or a runner outside
# Actions entirely all work — the executor's whole interface is issue read/write
# plus the repo at HEAD.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:
        description: 'How many dead runs this chain has continued through — set by the continuation job below, never by hand'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A label event on anything else is not this workflow's business — and a
    # workflow_dispatch carries no label at all, so it always runs.
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # The old cap — ≤ the engine's executing leash — retired with the heartbeat
    # (§15.15). A run is bounded by ONE work step now, and a holder that is alive
    # says so on its item every 15 minutes, so the leash reclaims silence rather
    # than length. What is left here is a backstop against a wedged runner, well
    # clear of any declared `code_work_timeout`.
    timeout-minutes: 350
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          # The operator hold (DESIGN §8): set this repo variable to `true` and
          # every entry point exits at its first act, having fired nothing.
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
          # The wiring converge stamps every declared required_secret, and every
          # configured invocation endpoint's token, below this marker — by name.
          # claudinite:secrets
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs

  # A run that dies — crash, timeout, cancellation, runner loss — never reaches
  # its own re-dispatch, so without this the queue would sit until the next cron
  # fire. The platform runs this job on a FRESH runner after any such death
  # (DESIGN §10, S36), and its one step fires that dispatch instead: the
  # remainder drains in ~a minute, while the dead run's OWN item waits for the
  # executing leash to reclaim it — nothing here touches that item.
  #
  # `continuation_depth` is the stop. A run that dies at startup — a broken
  # engine, a revoked token — dies identically every time, and an unguarded
  # continuation would dispatch itself for as long as that lasts. After three the
  # chain stops and SAYS SO on the repo's workflow-failure issue: a queue that has
  # quietly stopped draining is the one failure nothing else here would surface,
  # since every individual run looks like an ordinary death.
  continue-the-chain:
    needs: execute
    if: failure() || cancelled()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const depth = Number('${{ inputs.continuation_depth }}' || 0) + 1;
            const ref = context.payload.repository?.default_branch
              ?? context.ref.replace('refs/heads/', '');
            const run = `${context.serverUrl}/${context.repo.owner}/${context.repo.repo}/actions/runs/${context.runId}`;
            if (depth <= 3) {
              await github.rest.actions.createWorkflowDispatch({
                owner: context.repo.owner,
                repo: context.repo.repo,
                workflow_id: 'claudinite-executor.yml',
                ref,
                inputs: { continuation_depth: String(depth) },
              });
              core.info(`the executor run died — dispatched a fresh one on ${ref} (continuation ${depth} of 3)`);
              return;
            }
            // The chain has died three times running: this is not one bad runner,
            // and dispatching a fourth would spend the day proving it. Escalate to
            // the same one-open-issue surface the scheduler's own failures use, and
            // let the hourly scheduler run be what tries again.
            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const title = 'Claudinite executor chain failed repeatedly';
            await github.rest.issues.createLabel({ owner, repo, name: 'workflow-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite scheduler: a scheduler run or task failed' }).catch(() => {});
            const body = `Three consecutive executor runs died before finishing their item. The chain stops here; the next hourly scheduler run will dispatch a fresh one.\n\nThe last run: ${run}`;
            const found = await github.rest.search.issuesAndPullRequests({ q: `repo:${owner}/${repo} is:issue is:open in:title "${title}"` });
            if (found.data.total_count > 0) await github.rest.issues.createComment({ owner, repo, issue_number: found.data.items[0].number, body });
            else await github.rest.issues.create({ owner, repo, title, labels: ['workflow-failure'], body });
            core.setFailed('the executor chain died three times in a row — escalated');
